Libertarian

/lib-er-TAIR-ee-uhn/ - the stress falls on TAIR · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Libertarian means advocating liberty and minimal government interference in people's choices.

His libertarian instincts surface whenever the city proposes a new permit — for food carts, for buskers, for anything.

Worked Example

The op-ed's libertarian case against the soda tax never mentions health: adults, it argues, may weigh their own risks at the corner store, and a government that prices their choices for them has slid from protecting liberty into managing lives.

Libertarian describes positions, streaks, and arguments that put personal liberty first and government second. It is not lawlessness: unlike the anarchist, who would abolish the state, the libertarian keeps it — small, fenced, and minding its own business.

How Libertarian Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

individualist

individualist: puts the single person before the group; libertarian aims that instinct at government power

permissive

permissive: easygoing about rules in general — a parent can be permissive; libertarian is a stance about the state

Antonyms

paternalist

paternalist: wants authority to manage people's choices for their own good

interventionist

interventionist: reaches for government action first, liberty later

How Strong Is It? — permissive → libertarian → anarchic

permissive vs. libertarian

permissive vs. libertarian: Permissive is milder than libertarian — an easygoing habit of allowing things, case by case, with no theory behind it.

anarchic vs. libertarian

anarchic vs. libertarian: Anarchic goes further than libertarian: the libertarian would cut government back to a sliver, while an anarchic program would do away with it — the position you'll meet on this unit's anarchist card.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of libertarian.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — libert

Root — libert: freedom (Latin libertas, from liber, free)

Suffix — -arian

Suffix — -arian: advocate of, believer in

Put it together

Put it together: Libert- (freedom, Latin libertas, from liber, 'free') + -arian (advocate of) = an advocate of freedom. The suffix builds believers out of principles — vegetarian, humanitarian — and this believer's principle is liberty.

Use the root in a new word: liberate

Use the root in a new word: liberate: The class project liberated a jar of ladybugs into the school garden at last bell.
